intentional

/in-TEN-shuh-nul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Intentional means done deliberately and on purpose, not by accident.

The referee ruled that the trip was intentional, not clumsy, and reached for the red card.

Example

During the chess tournament, Priya gave up her queen, and gasps went around the room. Spectators assumed she had blundered away her strongest piece. Three moves later, her remaining pieces closed around her opponent's king, and everyone understood that the sacrifice had been entirely intentional. She had surrendered her queen on purpose, as one step in a plan of her own making.

Priya gave up her queen deliberately and on purpose as part of a plan, not by accident, which is exactly what intentional means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

deliberate: Deliberate means done consciously and on purpose, and it often adds slowness and care — a deliberate pause, deliberate steps. Intentional is the plainer legal-and-everyday word for the same on-purpose quality, defined against accident. A speech is delivered in a deliberate tone; a foul is ruled intentional.

purposeful: Purposeful means done with a clear aim in mind, and it praises direction and drive — a purposeful stride, purposeful work. Intentional settles only one question: the act was chosen, not accidental. A wandering conversation can still be intentional; only one guided by an aim is purposeful.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

accidental: happening by chance rather than on purpose

inadvertent: done without meaning to or noticing

Where it sits · how much planning lies behind the act

conscious → intentional → premeditated

conscious vs. intentional: A conscious act is one a person is merely aware of doing, while an intentional act is chosen on purpose to achieve something.

premeditated vs. intentional: An intentional act is done on purpose in the moment, but a premeditated act is planned out carefully ahead of time.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-: toward

Root — tent: from Latin tendere, to stretch

Suffix — -ion: the act or state of

Suffix — -al: relating to

Put it together: Intentional is built on Latin intendere, 'to stretch toward,' from in- (toward) plus tendere (to stretch). An intentional act is one your mind has already stretched toward: you aimed at it on purpose before you did it.

Use the root in a new word: tension: You could feel the tension in the tightrope, the same Latin stretching, tendere, that hides inside the word intentional.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral; everyday and legal register

Intentional draws its force from the contrast with accidental. Courts, referees, and teachers all lean on that line: the same act, a shove, a spill, a deleted file, is judged very differently depending on whether it was intentional. Use it for actions, choices, and effects, not for people themselves.
